title: Crews rush to 'deliberate' fire at former RAF base in Hunts village
content: Firefighters rushed to a "deliberate" fire at a derelict former RAF base in a Huntingdonshire village. Crews were called to the former RAF Upwood site on Ramsey Road near Bury on Saturday, November 21, at 3.31pm. The base opened in 1917 after a nearby farm was requisitioned for use as an emergency landing ground. Standing mostly derelict since 1994, the site has been the target of fly tipping and arson attacks for a number of years. However, there have been plans to redevelop areas into community facilities. Crews from Ramsey arrived to find a blaze on the ground floor of the derelict building and used a hose reel to extinguish it. They returned to the station by 4.10pm. A statement from Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service reads: "The cause of the fire is believed to be deliberate." Anyone with information should contact Cambridgeshire Police via their website, quoting incident 445 of November 21. Alternatively, call Crimestoppers on 0800 555111.

title: New café and bistro on the cards for Huntingdonshire town
content: A new café and bistro could be on the cards for Ramsey if plans are approved. Turquazze Restaurant Ltd has submitted a fresh premises licence application to Huntingdonshire District Council. Bloom and Brew would operate from the unit previously occupied by Konak Café and Grill, on 34 Great Whyte. According to the applicant, the bistro would serve breakfast, lunch and dinner, including British and Mediterranean cuisine. "The premises has approximately 70 customer seats. Alcohol will be served indoors only, with meals, by waiter service at tables. "No off-sales of alcohol are proposed," the plans said. "Bloom and Brew will operate as a family-friendly café and restaurant. "Alcohol will only be served with meals, by waiter service at tables, staff will be trained in responsible alcohol sales, public safety and child protection. "The premises will be properly managed and supervised." If approved, the venue would serve alcohol for consumption on the premises between the hours of 8am and 10.30pm Monday to Sunday. content: CIL - Community Infrastructure Levy What is CIL? Community Infrastructure Levy, commonly referred to as CIL, is money collected by Huntingdonshire District Council from certain new developments. The funding is then used to help provide or improve infrastructure needed as communities grow. The money collected is broadly divided into three areas: Up to 5% can be retained by Huntingdonshire District Council towards the administration and collection of CIL. 15% is normally allocated to the Town or Parish Council for the area where the development takes place. Once an adopted Neighbourhood Plan is in place, this increases to 25%. Most of the remaining funding is retained by Huntingdonshire District Council for larger strategic infrastructure projects across the district. Ramsey Town Council currently receives the 15% neighbourhood portion. Once the Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan is adopted, this will increase to 25%, giving the Council a greater share of money from qualifying development to invest back into our communities. Current projects supported or earmarked through Ramsey Town Council’s CIL funding include: Improvements at The Moorings. Contributions towards Local Highways Improvement projects. Improvements to Newtown Road Play Park. Improvements to the public toilets. New benches at the skate park. CCTV at The Moorings and New Road. The Double Yellow Lines project. The Town Council is also considering future projects, including additional parking behind the doctor’s surgery at Mews Close. Local Highways Initiative Bid (LHI): what is an LHI? The Local Highway Improvement programme allows local councils and community organisations to apply to Cambridgeshire County Council for funding towards highway improvements. Projects can include new or extended footpaths, traffic-calming measures, speed-reduction schemes, and other changes designed to improve road and pedestrian safety. Ramsey Town Council identifies potential projects and submits applications to Cambridgeshire County Council. Applications are assessed by the County Council and, if successful, funding is awarded towards the cost of the scheme. Under the current scheme, up to £25,000 can be awarded towards more complex projects, with applicants expected to contribute at least 10% of the overall cost. One recent LHI project was the extension of the footpath along Stocking Fen Road towards the industrial estate, improving pedestrian access for people travelling to and from work. The Council has also submitted an application for speed-reduction measures on the approach to Ramsey St Mary’s and is awaiting the outcome. Abbey College Road Safety Campaign Abbey College students are raising funds towards the £10,000 needed to help pay for speed reduction measures on Hollow Lane. Students have been campaigning, the school submitted an LHI bid, and speed cushions are planned. They would be grateful if you could spare the price of a coffee and scan the QR code.

title: Hunts man charged with seven counts of rape named for first time
content: A man from Huntingdonshire charged with rape and intentional strangulation is due in court. Toby Tiller, of Princes Street, Ramsey, is due to appear at Huntingdon Magistrates' Court for his first hearing on Tuesday (November 17). He faces seven counts of raping a woman aged 16 years of age or older and two counts of intentional strangulation. The 24-year-old is also accused of engaging in controlling or coercive behaviour in an intimate relationship. The alleged offences all said to have occurred in Cambridgeshire between August 2024 and May 2025. Have you got a story you want to share? title: Motorcyclist seriously injured after crash involving Audi in Hunts town
content: A motorcyclist has been seriously injured in a crash involving a car in a Huntingdonshire town. Police were called at 4.47pm on Saturday (November 14) to reports of a collision between an Audi Q3 and a motorbike in Great Whyte, Ramsey. Officers and paramedics attended and the motorcyclist was rushed to hospital with serious injuries, Cambridgeshire Constabulary confirmed. A spokesperson for the force said: "The Audi driver was unhurt and remained at the scene. "An investigation is ongoing, and anyone with information should contact us via the website or 101 quoting incident 360 of November 14." Have you got a story you want to share? title: Reform councillor complains to Parliament over MP’s response to 199-home plan
content: A Reform UK councillor has complained to Parliament about MP Sam Carling over a 199-home development between Ramsey and Bury. Cllr Karan Maheshwari, who represents Ramsey on Huntingdonshire District Council, has submitted a complaint to the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards. It concerns North West Cambridgeshire MP Mr Carling’s response to Cllr Maheshwari’s request for him to intervene in planning application 25/01382/OUT, for 199 homes between Ramsey and Bury. A copy seen by this publication is dated November 2 and marked “DRAFT – NOT SUBMITTED”, but Cllr Maheshwari later confirmed he submitted it on November 3 and received confirmation on November 4. The dispute began after Huntingdonshire District Council’s development management committee said it was minded to reject the scheme. title: Here is some of Huntingdonshire's most unusual bridges and where to find them
content: From a medieval bridge with its own chapel to a 55-arch causeway, Huntingdonshire is packed with unusual crossings. The district’s rivers, floodplains and Fenland waterways have shaped travel for centuries, leaving medieval crossings and Fen drainage bridges behind. Here are some of Huntingdonshire’s most striking bridges and where to find them. St Ives Bridge One of the county’s most extraordinary bridges spans the River Great Ouse at St Ives. The town’s first bridge was built of wood in 1107, before work began on a stone replacement in the early 15th century. The stone crossing was completed in 1425, and a chapel was added the following year. It is one of only three bridges in England with a chapel. The bridge also still bears the scars of the English Civil War. Parliamentary troops destroyed part of it to hinder Royalist forces, so a temporary drawbridge was installed. When the damaged section was rebuilt in 1716, it was given rounded arches instead of matching the pointed medieval ones, leaving a visible difference today.
